Born in the late 19th century and often hurled as an insult, this contested political stance pits the so-called 'common people' against a perceived elite — what is it?
Populism: Political ideology emphasising the "common people"
A war correspondent in Afghanistan and Angola in the 1980s, this Oxford-educated Polish statesman later became his country's Foreign Minister and, since 2025, also Deputy Prime Minister — who is he?
Radosław Sikorski: Polish politician and journalist (born 1963)
This Congress politician led his party to victory in the 2023 election and became the second Chief Minister of Telangana — who is he?
Revanth Reddy: Chief Minister of Telangana (born 1969)
Raised in Russian-ruled Poland in a secular Jewish family, this Marxist theorist co-founded the anti-war Spartacus League and is remembered as a champion of socialist democracy — who is she?
A Harvard graduate and second cousin to a future U.S. president, this Boston revolutionary founded the Sons of Liberty and signed the Declaration of Independence — who was he?
Samuel Adams: Founding Father of the United States (1722–1803)
This Neo-Assyrian king destroyed Babylon in 689 BC and rebuilt Nineveh into a grand capital, but is most famous in the Hebrew Bible for his campaign in the Levant. Who was he?
Sennacherib: King of Assyria. Shortly after Sennacherib inherited the throne in 705 BC, Marduk-apla-iddina retook Babylon and allied with the Elamites.

During the Congo Crisis in 1961, a company of Irish UN peacekeepers was surrounded for five days by Katangese forces near a mining town before surrendering for lack of ammunition and water — which battle is this?
Siege of Jadotville: 1961 battle between Irish UN troops and Katanga during Congo Crisis.
Stepping out of his family's iron-and-steel business and into Parliament, this Conservative dominated British politics between the wars, serving as prime minister three separate times — who was he?
Stanley Baldwin: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom (1923–1924; 1924–1929; 1935–1937)

Fought from 1992 to 1997, this Central Asian conflict pitted rebels from the Garm and Gorno-Badakhshan regions, organized as the United Tajik Opposition, against a Russian-backed government — which conflict was it?
Tajikistani Civil War: Armed conflict in Tajikistan from 1992 to 1997.
Chief minister who engineered Henry VIII's break from Rome to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, this powerful statesman was beheaded in 1540 — a loss the king later regretted. Who was he?
After leading Turkey's main miners' union and briefly working at the World Bank, this engineer-turned-statesman served as prime minister before becoming president from 1989 to 1993 — who is he?
Turgut Özal: President of Turkey from 1989 to 1993. ANAP won a parliamentary majority in the 1983 general election and Özal subsequently became the prime minister of Turkey.

Serving as Argentina's 38th vice president since 2023, this conservative politician founded a legal-studies center focused on terrorism victims and belongs to the La Libertad Avanza coalition — who is she?
Victoria Villarruel: Vice President of Argentina since 2023. Villarruel denies such accusations, maintaining that she does not support the "National Reorganization Process".
Sparked by a dispute over Maria Theresa's right to inherit the Habsburg throne, this 1740–1748 conflict began when Prussia seized the wealthy province of Silesia — what was this conflict called?
War of the Austrian Succession: 1740–1748 war between European powers.

Known as the 'Mother of the Nation,' this South African anti-apartheid activist and politician served in parliament and led the ANC Women's League after marrying the country's future president in 1958 — who is she?
Winnie Mandela: South African activist and politician (1936–2018)

After helping secure the Qing dynasty's abdication, this Chinese general became the Republic's first formal president, only to declare himself emperor in 1915 and abdicate again months later — who was he?
Yuan Shikai: First president of the Republic of China (1859–1916)
Which of these people was born first?
Frank Kameny (born 1925) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is the eldest?
Ada Lovelace (born 1815) is the earliest of the four. Lovelace is often considered the first computer programmer.
Pascal (programming language) (founded 1970) is the earliest of the four.
C (programming language) (founded 1972) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below is best known as an astronomer?
Arthur Eddington is an astronomer. Sir Arthur Stanley Eddington (28 December 1882 – 22 November 1944) was an English astrophysicist and mathematician.
Which one below is best known as a mathematician?
Shakuntala Devi is a mathematician. Shakuntala Devi (4 November 1929 – 21 April 2013) was an Indian mental calculator, astrologer, and writer, popularly known as the "Human Computer".
What is the atomic number of Xenon?
Xenon is a chemical element; it has symbol Xe and atomic number 54.
What is the atomic number of Unbibium?
Unbibium, also known as element 122 or eka-thorium, is a hypothetical chemical element; it has placeholder symbol Ubb and atomic number 122.
In what year was Mario Molina born?
Mario Molina: Mario José Molina-Pasquel Henríquez (19 March 1943 – 7 October 2020) was a Mexican physical chemist.
In what year was Nikolai Patrushev born?
Nikolai Patrushev: Patrushev has spoken favorably of the rise of KGB stalwarts to the highest echelons of power of Russia, referring to them as the "new nobility".
In what year was Johannes Gutenberg born?
Johannes Gutenberg: Johannes Gensfleisch zur Laden zum Gutenberg (c. 1393–1406 – 3 February 1468) was a German inventor and craftsman who invented the movable-type printing press.
In what year did Ferruccio Lamborghini die?
Ferruccio Lamborghini: In 1959, he opened an oil burner factory, Lamborghini Bruciatori, which later entered the business of producing air conditioning equipment.
In what year did Archimedes die?
Archimedes died during the siege of Syracuse, when he was killed by a Roman soldier despite orders that he should not be harmed.
In what year was Hydrogen discovered?
Hydrogen is a chemical element; it has the symbol H and atomic number 1.
Mil Mi-8: Mil Moscow Helicopter Plant. The Mi-8 is the world's most-produced helicopter, with over 17,000 units used by over 50 countries.
Semen: prostate. Semen, also known as seminal fluid, is a bodily fluid that contains spermatozoa from the male gonads of animals.
In which country is Thalidomide scandal?
Thalidomide scandal: Germany. It was introduced as a sedative and medication for morning sickness without having been tested on pregnant women.
Who is credited with discovering Flerovium?
Flerovium: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research. Flerovium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Fl and atomic number 114.
Who is credited with discovering Hypochlorous acid?
Hypochlorous acid: Antoine Jérôme Balard. Hypochlorous acid is an inorganic compound with the chemical formula ClOH, also written as HClO, HOCl, or ClHO.
Who is credited with discovering Gallium?
Gallium: Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran. Gallium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ga and atomic number 31.
Sometimes called ajowan caraway or carom, this annual herb in the carrot family produces a seed-like fruit often confused with lovage — what is it?
Ajwain (Trachyspermum ammi) - also known as ajowan caraway, thymol seeds, bishop's weed, or carom - is an annual herb in the family Apiaceae.

With more than 140 species spread across 16 genera in oceans worldwide, these small forage fish are usually classified as oily fish, and a few South American species live only in fresh water — name this fish?
Anchovy are small, common forage fish of the family Engraulidae.
Native to Europe and Asia, which genus of burdock plants owes its seed-dispersal success to burrs that later inspired a famous fastening invention?
Arctium is a genus of biennial plants commonly known as burdock, family Asteraceae.
This American physicist shared the 2017 Nobel with Rainer Weiss and Kip Thorne for decisive contributions to LIGO and the observation of gravitational waves — who is he?
Barry Barish (born January 27, 1936) is an American experimental physicist and Nobel Laureate.

Thought to be the world's most abundant bird of prey in its family, with an estimated 6.7 million individuals, this opportunistic raptor is known for its angled wings and distinctive forked tail — what is it?
Black kite (Milvus migrans) is a medium-sized bird of prey in the family Accipitridae, which also includes many other diurnal raptors.
Meaning 'thunder lizard' in Greek, this sauropod dinosaur genus was described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1879 from a partial, skull-less skeleton found in Wyoming's Como Bluff — what dinosaur is it?

Brontosaurus (literally 'thunder lizard', from the Greek words bront, 'thunder', and saros, 'lizard') is a genus of herbivorous sauropod dinosaur that lived in present-day United States during the Late Jurassic period.
From starch that stores energy to the cellulose that stiffens plants and the chitin in insect shells, this biomolecule family is essentially sugars and their derivatives — what is it?
Carbohydrate is a sugar (saccharide) or a sugar derivative.

The smallest recognized dog breed in the world, this Mexican toy breed has large erect ears and a rounded skull, and its genes carry a trace of pre-Columbian indigenous American dog ancestry — which breed?

Chihuahua (dog breed) is a Mexican breed of toy dog and the smallest recognized dog breed in the world. It is primarily kept as a companion animal and is characterized by its compact size, large erect ears, and rounded skull.
Native to Africa, Arabia and India, this semi-succulent herb smells like oregano and is known by names like Spanish thyme and Mexican mint — which plant?
Coleus amboinicus is a species of semi-succulent perennial plant in the family Lamiaceae.

This interdisciplinary field, whose name combines a Latin word for 'accusation' with a Greek suffix meaning 'study of,' draws on sociology, psychology, economics, and law to examine crime and deviant behavior. What field is this?
Criminology (from Latin crimen, 'accusation', and Ancient Greek -, -logia, from logos, 'word, reason') is the interdisciplinary study of crime and deviant behaviour.
This colourless, highly volatile, sweet-smelling organic compound with formula (CH3CH2)2O was once used as a general anesthetic and remains a common laboratory solvent — what is it?

This American theoretical physicist, a professor emeritus at Princeton's Institute for Advanced Study, is renowned for foundational contributions to string theory and topological quantum field theory — who is he?
Edward Witten (born August 26, 1951) is an American theoretical physicist known for his contributions to string theory, topological quantum field theory, and various areas of mathematics.
The major female sex hormone, this estrogen steroid drives the development of breasts and a female pattern of fat distribution and regulates the menstrual cycle — which one is it?
Estradiol (E2), also called oestrogen, oestradiol, is an estrogen steroid hormone and the major female sex hormone.

Sometimes mistakenly called a cat despite belonging to the weasel family, this North American forest-dwelling carnivore is the only living species in its genus and is larger than the martens it resembles — what animal is it?
Fisher (animal) (Pekania pennanti) is a carnivorous mammal native to North America, a forest-dwelling creature whose range covers much of the boreal forest in Canada to the northern United States.
Practitioners of this discipline monitor crustal motion, tides, and polar shifts to maintain accurate global positioning reference frames — what is this field called?
Geodesy (jee-) or geodetics is the science of measuring and representing the geometry, gravity, and spatial orientation of the Earth in temporally varying 3D space.
One of only two wild camelid species native to South America, this llama relative lives at lower elevations than its cousin, the vicuña — what is it called?
Guanaco (gwah-; Lama guanicoe) is a camelid native to South America, closely related to the domesticated llama.
Never approved by any drug regulator, this THC-like compound made by hydrogenating cannabis isomers has been sold in head-shop vaporizers since the early 2020s — what is it?
Hexahydrocannabinol (HHC) is a phytocannabinoid that has been reported as a minor component of Cannabis oleoresin.
About the size of an almond in humans, this small brain region links the nervous system to the endocrine system via the pituitary gland — what is it?
Hypothalamus (pl.: hypothalami; from Ancient Greek (hup) 'under' and (thlamos) 'chamber') is a small part of the vertebrate brain that contains a number of nuclei with a variety of functions.
Serving as president of the European Commission from 1985 to 1995, this French politician played a central role in creating the European single market and laying groundwork for the euro — who is he?
Jacques Delors (20 July 1925 - 27 December 2023) was a French politician who served as president of the European Commission from 1985 to 1995.
Named after a 19th-century English physicist, this SI unit of energy equals the work done when a one-newton force moves an object one metre in the direction of that force — name the unit?
Joule (JOOL, or JOWL; symbol: J) is the unit of energy in the International System of Units (SI).
What reddish-brown, alcohol-based tincture of opium, roughly 10% opium by weight, was historically sold without a prescription as a pain reliever and cough suppressant until the early 20th century?
Laudanum is a tincture of opium containing approximately 10% powdered opium by weight (the equivalent of 1% morphine).
Used since pre-Columbian times as a pack animal that can haul about a quarter of its body weight for miles, which domesticated South American camelid has wool low in lanolin?
Llama (Spanish) (Lama glama) is a domesticated South American camelid, widely used as a meat and pack animal by Andean cultures since the pre-Columbian era.
Though it's the strongest bone in the face, this lower jawbone tends to deform with age and is prone to fractures — what is it called?

Mandible (from the Latin mandibula, 'for chewing'), lower jaw, or jawbone is a bone that makes up the lower - and typically more mobile - component of the mouth (the upper jaw being known as the maxilla).

Patented in 1922 and used to relieve pain, fever, and spasms, this drug's sale is restricted in some countries due to a rare but serious blood-cell side effect discovered in the 1970s — what drug is it?
Metamizole is a painkiller, spasm reliever, and fever reliever drug.
Found naturally in the dark resin of opium and given everywhere from pills to spinal injections, this opiate alters how the brain feels pain — what is it?
Morphine is an opiate found naturally in opium, a dark brown resin produced by drying the latex of opium poppies (Papaver somniferum).
This multidisciplinary field studies the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves — their function and their disorders — blending physiology, anatomy, and more — name the field?
Neuroscience is the scientific study of the nervous system (the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nervous system), its functions, and its disorders.
In this learning process, voluntary behaviors grow more frequent through reinforcement or fade through punishment and extinction — what is it called?
Operant conditioning is a learning process in which voluntary behaviors are modified by association with the addition (or removal) of reward or aversive stimuli.
Combining medicine with comedy, this physician organizes volunteers to clown around for orphans and patients worldwide through a nonprofit institute he founded in 1989 — who is he?
Patch Adams (born May 28, 1945) is an American physician, comedian, social activist, clown, and author.
Ranging in color from clear to yellow, green, or even grey, this respiratory mucus is expelled through coughing and also goes by the name sputum — what is it?
Phlegm (Ancient) is mucus produced by the respiratory system, excluding that produced by the throat and nose passages.
Abundant throughout the plant kingdom, this broad class of naturally occurring phenolic compounds includes flavonoids and ellagitannin — what is the family called?
Polyphenol are a large family of naturally occurring phenols.

This psychiatric state describes an inability to distinguish reality from delusion, marked by symptoms like hallucinations and disorganized thinking, and can stem from conditions like schizophrenia or bipolar disorder — name the state?
Psychosis is the inability to distinguish what is or is not real.
One of the three ancient arts of discourse alongside grammar and logic, this discipline studies the techniques speakers and writers use to inform, persuade, and motivate an audience — what is it?
Rhetoric is the art of persuasion.
Which plant genus in the mint family, comprising nearly 1,000 species of shrubs and perennials, includes both a common cooking herb and — surprisingly — rosemary as one of its species?
Salvia is the largest genus of plants in the sage family Lamiaceae, with just under 1,000 species of shrubs, herbaceous perennials, and annuals.
Until 2010, this pungent little cultivar of the onion was classified as its own species before being folded back into the common onion — name this allium?
Shallot is a cultivar group of the onion. Until 2010, the (French red) shallot was classified as a separate species, Allium ascalonicum.
This circular muscle normally maintains constriction of a natural body passage, relaxing only as physiological function requires — what is it called?
Sphincter is a circular muscle that normally maintains constriction of a natural body passage or orifice and relaxes as required by normal physiological functioning.
Encompassing domestic pigs and their ancestor the Eurasian wild boar, this genus within the even-toed ungulate family Suidae is native across Eurasia and Africa — which genus?

Sus (genus) is the genus of domestic and wild pigs, within the even-toed ungulate family Suidae. Sus includes domestic pigs (Sus domesticus) and their ancestor, the common Eurasian wild boar (Sus scrofa), along with various other species.

Governed by four fundamental laws relating heat, work and temperature to energy and entropy, this branch of physics underpins chemical, mechanical and biochemical engineering alike — which field of physics?
Thermodynamics is a branch of physics that deals with heat, work, and temperature, and their relation to energy, entropy, and the physical properties of matter and radiation.
One of the earliest arthropod groups ever to appear in the fossil record, this extinct marine creature persisted in the oceans for nearly 270 million years across over 22,000 species — what is it?
Trilobite (meaning "three-lobed entities") are extinct marine arthropods that form the class Trilobita.
Its wild form is dioecious while domesticated versions bear hermaphrodite flowers — this Mediterranean-native plant is the ancestor of nearly all wine and table varieties — what species?

Vitis vinifera is a species of flowering plant, native to the Mediterranean region, Central Europe, and southwestern Asia, from Morocco and Portugal north to southern Germany and east to northern Iran.
Almost always found combined with lanthanide minerals and never on its own in nature, this element with symbol Y is a key ingredient in the phosphors used inside LEDs — which element?
Yttrium is a chemical element; it has symbol Y and atomic number 39.

The only legitimate child of the poet Lord Byron, this English mathematician saw that Charles Babbage's analytical engine could do far more than crunch numbers — earning her a reputation as the first computer programmer. Who was she?
Shining as the brightest star in Taurus some 67 light-years from Earth, this red giant has swollen to roughly 45 times the Sun's size despite a cooler surface — which star?
Aldebaran: Taurus Brightest Star. Aldebaran (Arabic: الدَّبَرَان, lit. 'The Follower') is a star in the zodiac constellation of Taurus.
Used to treat dangerous heart rhythms like ventricular fibrillation, which drug can take weeks to work when swallowed but carries risks of lung, liver, thyroid, and eye toxicity?
Awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2008 for his AIDS-relief work on PEPFAR, this immunologist directed the U.S. allergy and infectious-disease institute from 1984 to 2022. Who is he?
A notoriously toxic metalloid and pnictogen with atomic number 33, it's used in lead alloys for car batteries and ammunition and as a semiconductor dopant — which element is it?
Arsenic: Chemical element with atomic number 33 (As). It is a metalloid and one of the pnictogens, and therefore shares many properties with its group 15 neighbors phosphorus and antimony.
This slender projection of a nerve cell typically carries electrical impulses away from the cell body toward other neurons, muscles, or glands — what is it called?
Axon: Long projection on a neuron that conducts signals to other neurons.
A colorless, sweet-smelling liquid hiding in petroleum, this ring-shaped hydrocarbon helps give gasoline its distinctive aroma — what is it?
Despite being just 12 to 20 cm long, this small marine creature's vivid markings flash brighter when it feels threatened, and its bite delivers a neurotoxin called tetrodotoxin — what is it?
Blue-ringed octopus: Four species of mollusk.

This tropical tree's moderately ripe flesh, once cooked, is said to taste like a fresh-baked loaf with a potato-like flavor, and 18th-century navigators carried it in seedless form to the Caribbean — what is it?
Breadfruit: Edible fruit-bearing tree in family. Moraceae.
This intensely sour citrus hybrid — a cross between a kumquat and likely a mandarin orange — is a staple of Philippine cooking and also popular in Malaysian and Indonesian cuisine — which fruit?
Calamansi: Hybrid species of citrus. Calamansi (Citrus × microcarpa), also known as calamondin, Philippine lime, or Philippine lemon, is a citrus hybrid cultivated predominantly in the Philippines.
Extracted from the cochineal insect, this bright-red pigment is also known by the food-additive code E120 — what is it called?
Carmine: Pigment, aluminium salt of carminic acid.
The biochemist hailed as the "father" of industrial fermentation, instrumental in the 1917 Balfour Declaration, became the first president of Israel — who was he?
Chaim Weizmann: Israeli statesman and British chemist (1874–1952)
Native to the Andean forests of South America, this genus of trees is nicknamed the 'fever tree' because its bark yields quinine, the only effective malaria treatment for centuries — what is it?
Cinchona: Genus of plants, source of quinine.
Used to treat gout, familial Mediterranean fever, and pericarditis, this medication has such a narrow therapeutic index that its injectable form was pulled from the US market in 2008. What is it?
Colchicine: Medication mainly used to treat gout. The American College of Rheumatology recommends colchicine, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or steroids in the treatment of gout.

Describing how closely two variables move together, this statistical measure is famously not proof of causation, and two variables can even be linked this way without truly depending on each other — what is it called?
Correlation: Statistical relationship. In statistics, correlation is a type of statistical relationship between two random variables or bivariate data.
Making up about 80 percent water and mostly colorless, this catch-all term covers everything inside a cell's outer membrane except its nucleus — what is it?
Cytoplasm: All of the contents of a cell including organelles but excluding the nucleus.

Marked by deep gasping breaths and breath that smells oddly fruity or like acetone, this life-threatening condition arises when a shortage of insulin forces the body to burn fat into acidic ketones — what is it?
Diabetic ketoacidosis: Medical condition. Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a potentially life-threatening acute complication of diabetes mellitus.
The tallest of the three camel species, standing up to 2.4 meters at the shoulder, which animal carries a single hump of fat on its back?
Native to southern India, this ginger-family plant produces the aromatic seeds used in both sweet and savory cooking — what is it, botanically?
Elettaria cardamomum: Species of flowering plant.
This fibromuscular tube carries food from throat to stomach using peristaltic contractions, and its name traces to Ancient Greek roots meaning roughly 'I carry what I ate.' What is it?
Esophagus: Vertebrate organ through which food passes to the stomach.

Derived from a Greek word meaning 'to lead out,' this scholarly practice of critically interpreting a text — often the Bible — also examines its historical background and literary genre — what is it called?
Exegesis: Critical investigation of a text.

Modern phylogenetics calls this a paraphyletic group covering nearly every vertebrate except the tetrapods — gill-bearing, limbless-of-digits, and usually cold-blooded. What aquatic animals are these?
Only chefs with three-plus years of rigorous training may legally prepare this potentially lethal Japanese pufferfish dish, whose poison is tetrodotoxin — what is it?
The largest of its family, this mostly solitary mammal uses long foreclaws to dig into nests and a sticky tongue to slurp up ants and termites — what animal is it?
Giant anteater: Species of mammal. The giant anteater (Myrmecophaga tridactyla) is an insectivorous mammal native to Central and South America.
Dating back roughly 250 million years to the early Triassic, this ground-dwelling insect hears through an organ on its abdomen and leaps away from danger using powerful hind legs — what is it?
Grasshopper: Common name for a group of insects.

This Austrian physician who coined "autistic psychopathy" lent his name to a syndrome, but later faced allegations he referred disabled children to a Vienna clinic that killed hundreds during the Nazi era — who was he?
Found in trace amounts in modern gasoline blends, this colorless, six-carbon alkane boils at about 69°C and serves as a cheap, low-reactivity solvent — what is it?
A colorless gas that throws off white fumes the moment it meets moist air, it turns into a familiar strong acid once dissolved in water — which compound, formula HCl?
Hydrogen chloride: Chemical compound. Hydrogen chloride gas and hydrochloric acid are important in technology and industry.
Equal to one-twelfth of a foot and derived from the Roman word for 'twelfth,' this unit of length has been pegged to exactly 25.4 millimeters since the mid-20th century — what is it?
Inch: Unit of length. The inch (symbol: in or ″) is a unit of length in the British Imperial and the United States customary systems of measurement.

The New York Times once called him "the nation's most influential evangelical leader," yet he was never an ordained minister — instead this psychologist founded Focus on the Family and led it from 1977 to 2010. Who was he?
James Dobson: American evangelical Christian psychologist and author (1936–2025)
Struggling with a morphine addiction from a Civil War saber wound, this pharmacist and chemist developed a coca-and-caffeine beverage in 1886 that became Coca-Cola — who is he?
John Stith Pemberton: American pharmacist, inventor of Coca-Cola (1831–1888)
First described in 1845 by a German physicist, these two equalities govern current and voltage in electrical networks and generalized Georg Ohm's work — what are they called?
Kirchhoff's circuit laws: Two equalities that deal with the current and potential difference.

Caused by a bacterium that thrives in fresh water and can contaminate hot tubs and water tanks, this atypical pneumonia brings cough, high fever and muscle pains days after exposure — what's it called?
Legionnaires' disease: Form of atypical pneumonia. Legionnaires' disease is a form of atypical pneumonia caused by any species of Legionella bacteria, quite often Legionella pneumophila.
Named after both a biblical sea monster and the author of 'Moby-Dick,' this extinct predatory sperm whale roamed ancient oceans roughly 9 million years ago — which genus?
Livyatan: Extinct genus of sperm whale from the Miocene epoch.
Native to northeastern Australia and first commercially grown at scale in Hawaii during the 1880s, this is the only widely cultivated food plant indigenous to Australia — what nut is it?
Macadamia: Genus of plants indigenous to Australia.
Kangaroos, koalas, and wombats all belong to this mammal group whose young are born undeveloped and finish developing in their mother's pouch — what group is it?
Marsupial: Infraclass of mammals in the clade Metatheria.
The only operational rocket-powered fighter ever fielded, this WWII German interceptor became the first piloted aircraft to exceed 1,000 km/h in level flight — which aircraft?

Messerschmitt Me 163 Komet: German rocket-powered interceptor. The Messerschmitt Me 163 Komet is a rocket-powered interceptor aircraft primarily designed and produced by the German aircraft manufacturer Messerschmitt.
Awarded the 1976 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, this University of Chicago economist championed monetarism over Keynesianism and mentored future laureates like Gary Becker — who is he?
Milton Friedman: American economist and statistician (1912–2006)
Produced by glands throughout the body's linings — including the respiratory, digestive, and urogenital tracts — which slippery substance traps and destroys harmful bacteria and viruses?
Mucus: Secretion produced by mucous membranes.

The Navy paid his Purdue aeronautical-engineering tuition under the Holloway Plan, and he flew the Grumman F9F Panther off the USS Essex in the Korean War before his most famous flight of all — which Ohio-born aviator was he?
A subsonic flying wing with a crew of two to three, this nuclear-capable stealth aircraft was built to slip past sophisticated air defenses for the US Air Force — what is it?
Northrop B-2 Spirit: American heavy strategic bomber.

Sitting between tissue and a full body system in life's hierarchy, this general term describes a structural unit built from functional tissue (parenchyma) plus supportive tissue (stroma), as seen in the intestinal wall — what is such a unit called?
Organ (biology): Collection of tissues with similar functions.
This skin sensation includes the classic 'pins and needles' feeling when a limb falls asleep, and can also be triggered by hitting your funny bone — what is it called?
Paresthesia: Dermal sensation with no physical cause.
In mathematics, what term describes both an ordered arrangement of a set's members and the act of rearranging them, as seen in the six possible orderings of three distinct numbers?
Permutation: Mathematical version of an order change.

A counting argument in mathematics: if you have more items than containers, at least one container must hold more than one item. Famous example: three gloves, but only two hand categories — what's this principle?
Pigeonhole principle: If there are more items than boxes holding them, one box must contain at least two items.
Looking like a jellyfish but actually a floating colony of cooperating zooids, this venomous siphonophore is also nicknamed the bluebottle — what is it?
Portuguese man o' war: Species of marine cnidarian.
This holotropical bird family comprises a dozen Afrotropical species and some 167 Neotropical species, including the blue-and-yellow macaw and the grey parrot — which family is this?
Psittacidae: Family of birds. The family Psittacidae or holotropical parrots is one of three families of true parrots.
After his Jewish family fled Germany, this engineer at Sanders Associates dreamed up playing games on a TV screen and built a 'Brown Box' that became the first home video game console — who is he?
Ralph H. Baer: American inventor and engineer (1922–2014)
This English anatomist coined the word 'Dinosauria' — 'terrible reptile' — yet remained an outspoken critic of Darwin's theory of natural selection — who is it?
Richard Owen: English biologist and palaeontologist (1804–1892)
Also known as brewer's or baker's yeast, this single-celled fungus believed to have originated on grape skins is one of biology's most-studied model organisms — which species?
Saccharomyces cerevisiae: Species of yeast. The species has been instrumental in winemaking, baking, and brewing since ancient times.
Comprising seven species from the flatback to the leatherback, five of these ocean-dwelling reptiles are threatened with extinction — what are they?
Sea turtle: Reptiles of the superfamily Chelonioidea.
Highly water-soluble and non-hygroscopic, this colorless compound with formula AgNO3 is the least expensive salt of its kind — which compound?
Silver nitrate: Chemical compound. It is highly water soluble colorless solid that is a precursor to many other silver compounds.
Combining vowel and consonant sounds into words for acts like persuading or declaring, this use of the human voice can even happen without any listener at all — what is it?
Speech: Human vocal communication using spoken language.
A bitter, colorless alkaloid from the seeds of the nux-vomica tree, it kills birds and rodents by triggering muscular convulsions and asphyxia. Which poison is it?
Strychnine: Poisonous substance used as pesticide.
Named after a figure from Greek mythology, this blue-gray transition metal with atomic number 73 is prized for corrosion resistance and shows up in capacitors inside computers. What element is this?
Tantalum: Chemical element with atomic number 73 (Ta)
